sec.title: Purpose of review
sec.p: The purpose of this review is to present an overview of principles of motor learning (PML) and summarize the most recent evidence regarding the application of PML to optimize voice therapy intervention.

sec.title: Recent findings
sec.p: The principles of motor learning that have been proven effective in sport, neuroscience, physical therapies and motor speech and swallowing therapies are now being demonstrated to be relevant and effective in voice therapy.

sec.title: Summary
sec.p: Current research is in its early stages with a small number of retrospective, prospective and experimental studies investigating aspects of practice, feedback, instruction and modelling. Low participant numbers are noted as a limitation in many studies. Research shows motor learning principles are effective, but large-scale studies are needed to develop a deeper understanding of how to optimise the PML in individual therapeutic scenarios.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Voice therapy is a requirement for the successful treatment of many voice disorders. The components of voice therapy are divided into two categories, both of which are used in most voice therapy interventions [1,2]. Indirect voice therapy focuses on education and behaviour change to reduce harmful voice-use, while direct voice therapy uses specific voice exercises to modify how the voice is produced [3]. Motor learning (ML) explains how humans acquire, refine, and retain complex motor skills over time [4]. From its origins in sport, ML emerged in the motor speech disorders literature in the early 1990s and the principles were formalized as a guiding framework in the following decade, especially within acquired apraxia of speech (AOS) and dysarthria [5,6]. PML were then synthesized specifically for speech rehabilitation [7▪▪] and then emerged in voice therapy contexts in the early 2000s with the work of Verdolini et al.[8,9] and Yiu et al.[10].

Principles of motor learning (PML) provides a framework for teaching and modifying motor behaviours through structured practice, stage-appropriate feedback schedules, task specificity, and an emphasis on long-term retention and generalization across related skills and contexts. PML targets goal-directed changes in motor tasks to achieve outcomes such as improved vocal quality, extended vocal range, or reduced laryngeal tension [11▪]. Crucially, ML differs from short-term performance gains because it produces relatively permanent improvements that support retention over time and transfer to new situations [7▪▪]. ML is goal-oriented, organized around functional outcomes such as vocal efficiency, clarity, ease, or projection, rather than isolated exercises, and is adaptive, enabling speakers to adjust voice use to varying demands (e.g., noise, duration, room size).

Motor learning is a dynamic, phased process involving motor, sensory, perceptual, and cognitive systems. It progresses through two interdependent phases – prepractice (skill acquisition) and practice (long term retention/generalization) – each requiring specific goals and strategies [4,7▪▪]. Although described as linear, the phases may overlap or occur concurrently across different tasks. In the prepractice phase, the priority is initial skill acquisition and because performance is fragile, learning is aided by explicit instruction, clinician modelling, and frequent feedback to build confidence and establish an accurate movement pattern. In this phase, the learner is inexperienced and highly attentive to both exogenous and endogenous feed-back to guide more accurate and successful movement production. Once the skill can be performed in a constrained set of conditions, therapy moves into the practice phase, which aims to provide high intensity, varied practice at high frequency. Gradually, adaptive context-sensitive motor control emerges through repeated and varied interaction between the organism and their environment. The continuous coupling of perception and action establishes the boundaries of accurate / successful movement execution (e.g. [12,13]. Practice may be supervised (often by a clinician in session) or independent (at home/work/etc.) (see Fig. 1).

caption.p: Motor learning progression in voice therapy from skill acquisition to generalization and transfer (based on Maas et al. 2008). Clinical principle: therapy should not remain in blocked, high-feedback practice. Durable voice change requires progression toward variable, externally focused, lower-feedback conditions that resemble real communication.

sec.p: Effective practice is structured to enhance long-term learning. Distributed practice (spaced sessions) supports better retention than massed practice [14]; varied practice across contexts (e.g., pitch, loudness, linguistic tasks) promotes transfer beyond therapy; and random order of practice reduces reliance on predictable order, stimulates both retrieval and execution, and improves adaptability [7▪▪]. Gradually reduced feedback builds self-monitoring and independent control. Successful learning is demonstrated through retention (performance after time without practice) and generalization (use across settings/partners).

sec.title: DESCRIPTIVE FRAMEWORKS OF PRINCIPLES OF MOTOR LEARNING IN VOICE THERAPY
sec.p: The first dedicated PML framework for voice therapy was described in 2010, with a focus on prepractice principles with examples and definitions [15▪] (see Fig. 2) McIlwaine et al. (2010) described three criteria for transitioning from prepractice to practice: understanding the target movement and how it should be produced; developing an internal reference of correctness to recognize accurate versus inaccurate performance; and performing the movement safely and correctly with clinician support.

caption.p: Principles of motor learning and voice therapy: the prepractice phase of therapy. Reproduced from McIlwaine A, Madill C, McCabe P. (2010).

sec.p: Iwarsson [16▪] went on to identify nine factors supporting stable voice-behaviour change: cue-altering, attention exercises, repetition, cognitive activation, negative practice, inhibition through interruption, decomposing complex behaviour, the ‘each time–every time’ principle, and successive implementation of automaticity to stabilize and habituate improved spontaneous speech. This work emphasized that effective voice therapy requires both acquiring new skills and inhibiting/replacing entrenched automatic habits supported by repetition/distributed practice, reduced feedback frequency, and cognitive effort. Tasks progress from high attentional control to automatic speech to improve adherence, reduce relapse, and strengthen long-term effects.

In 2020, the Motor Learning Classification Framework (MLCF) defined prepractice elements found in the literature in more detail [11▪]. It listed 65 ML elements, found in published literature, for acquiring a new skill and establishing an accurate movement pattern. Clinician behaviours (motivation, modelling, verbal information, feedback) were coded by nine clinicians in three voice therapy training videos Intra-rater reliability was good with inter-rater high for modelling/verbal information but lower for motivation/feedback. Overall, the MCLF captured most behaviours demonstrating that PML can be operationalized to identify clinician–client interactions. The MCLF was later used to compare speech-language pathology students and experienced clinicians [17]. Verbal-information proportions were found to be similar. Experienced clinicians used more behaviours that the raters identified as problem-solving, and, uniquely, showed repeated sequences including perceptual training. Both groups showed more verbal explanation than modelling.

Van Stan et al. developed a Taxonomy of Voice Therapy that distinguishes indirect and direct interventions delivered through extrinsic and/or intrinsic methods and includes a dictionary of taxonomy terms referencing numerous PML elements [18▪]. The Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) system references motor learning principles but focuses on behavioural therapies as ingredients, targets, and mechanisms of action [19]. Applied to voice therapy (RTSS-Voice), it showed strong content validity and enabled clear comparison of ingredients, targets, and mechanisms across four treatments [20▪▪].

Frameworks such as the MLCF and RTSS-Voice have identified that all voice therapies include elements of ML, but many therapies are insufficiently described in the literature to determine which specific principles are applied. Given that systematic reviews show that no one voice therapy is consistently superior to others [4,5], clinicians must decide how best to apply PML to the individual patient in front of them. What then is known about the rationale and efficacy of different PML elements in voice therapy?

sec.title: PRE-PRACTICE
sec.p: Prepractice has been identified as comprising 5 key components that support early learning (see Fig. 2). Motivation is foundational, and lack of motivation is a major barrier to therapy engagement and success [21]. Because motivation drives attention, effort, and persistence, therapists should build engagement by linking tasks to what is meaningful to the client and aligning targets with the client's goals and priorities [15▪]. Motivation can be strengthened by tying activities to SMART goals [22], keeping tasks appropriately challenging, and using the client's own language to increase ownership. Rubino, Dietrich, and Verdolini Abbott [23▪] argue that identity is central to motivation in voice habilitation/rehabilitation because vocal change can feel either self-consistent, supporting help-seeking, adherence, and maintenance, or self-threatening, subsequently reducing these behaviours. Aldridge-Waddon and Russell [24▪] likewise recommended Compassion Focused Therapy-informed voice strategies to reduce threat responses and sustain engagement and motivation/adherence.

Instruction and verbal information help clients understand what to do and why it matters, via clear performance instructions, links to functional goals, and perceptual training to attend to cues (vocal quality, loudness, effort). Instructions can be implicit e.g. having the clinician model with an expected attempt to copy from the client; or explicit, e.g. verbal or written instructions to perform specific tasks such as ‘raise your tongue into the ‘ng’ position’. Focus of attention is defined as being either internal, where the patient focuses on their own body movements to perform the skill, e.g. ‘lower the larynx with a yawn feeling’, or external, where the patient focuses on the outcome of the movement [25], e.g. ‘notice how clear the sound is’. This definition needs some clarification for voice therapy as often the outcome of a movement is a sensation internally felt. Instructions such as ‘notice a feeling of buzzing on the lips’ or ‘notice the widening in the throat’ seem to involve both internal and external focus of attention as they are outcomes of an internal muscular movement.

Implicit, explicit, and combinations of both implicit and explicit instruction, and internal or external focus of attention have demonstrated different effects on performance in the session versus longer-term learning. In a study of 30 healthy adults acquiring and practicing oral versus nasalized phrases, weekly for four weeks [26▪], nasometry revealed that instruction affected phrase-level gains. Explicit and integrated cues were similarly effective at initial acquisition in session 1, but thereafter integrated cues resulted in greater retention than explicit or implicit cues alone. For nasalized phrases, variability differed by instruction but pairwise tests were nonsignificant. Explicit, internally focused cues improved immediate accuracy but did not consistently enhance retention posttherapy, suggesting that cue wording and structure influence acquisition, generalization, and durability. Similarly, effective cross-disciplinary teaching of straw phonation used demonstration, rationale, graded progression, reinforcement, and self-assessment, whereas vague/excessive talk, unclear goals, over-demonstration, and poor monitoring, reduced acquisition [27].

Modelling is considered essential in the prepractice stage. Therapist demonstrations provide concrete auditory and visual examples of the target behaviour and may support implicit learning by giving clients a reliable reference. The Imitation Model (IM; clinician demonstrates, patient imitates) was compared with the Verbal Instructions Model (VIM), which uses structured verbal cues to support patient exploration [28], in a prospective trial of 56 adults with functional voice disorders. Both methods significantly improved outcomes after the prepractice stage at follow-up. VIM showed greater long-term gains (total Voice Handicap Index (VHI) and physical/emotional subscales at 6–12 months) and better immediate perceptual voice quality. Groups did not differ in hoarseness, fatigue, or long-term Voice Range Profile change [29▪]. To investigate whether verbal instructions improve learning from video/aural modelling for a complex voice task (’vocal siren’) without external feedback, 30 participants were randomized to model + verbal instruction versus model only and completed 40 trials [30]. Outcomes (five time points) included phonation time, intensity, cepstral peak prominence, peak-to-peak time, and root mean square error. The instruction plus modelling group improved on more measures, especially vocal intensity. Neither group matched the model nor retained the skill after 1 day, suggesting 40 feedback-free trials were insufficient.

Perceptual training is needed in ML because learners must perceive the specific movement features they are trying to change and/or acquire [31]. This emphasis is reflected across voice therapy models and frameworks. Most programmes and techniques combine strategies that raise awareness of the feel of voice production (kinaesthetic/interoceptive cues) and the sound quality produced (auditory cues), with variations such as detecting voice onset type and resonance. Consistent with sensorimotor models of voice production, evidence suggests that perceptual responsiveness during stimulability may indicate treatment readiness and guide therapy tailoring, within a PML framework. Patients’ self-perceived auditory ('sound’) and kinaesthetic (‘feel’) awareness was found to relate to outcomes from Conversation Training Therapy (CTT) for muscle tension dysphonia and benign vocal fold lesions [32▪]. Those who perceived improvements in the feeling of voice production in stimulability testing (thus in the prepractice phase) showed faster, clinically meaningful VHI-10 reductions, though between-group differences were not statistically significant.

Feedback in prepractice is typically frequent and immediate, emphasizing knowledge of performance (KP) i.e. feedback about how the movement was produced. Knowledge of results (KR) indicates only if the attempt was correct or incorrect. KP helps clients build an internal reference of correctness and adjust inaccurate patterns before they are reinforced [33,34]. Early learning of a complex vocal siren task in 36 untrained young adult women randomized to receive either KR; (accuracy- or model-based) or KP; (auditory ‘how it sounded,’ kinaesthetic ‘how it felt’) through scripted terminal feedback in a single ~15-min session, demonstrated that all groups improved. KP produced the greatest gains in vocal intensity, with combined auditory and kinaesthetic KP outperforming KR [34]. Significantly, kinaesthetic KP best preserved vocal clarity. No timing advantage was observed, and the study was limited by the absence of a no-feedback control group and the use of a nonclinical sample.

sec.title: PRACTICE
sec.p: In the practice phase, the goal shifts from acquiring the new skill to making it consistent, durable, and transferable beyond the clinic. Practice structure becomes especially important for long-term retention. Distributed practice, in which training is spaced over time rather than condensed into long blocks, is more effective for maintaining gains than massed practice [35]. Varied practice further supports learning by requiring clients to use the skill under different conditions such as across different speaking tasks, volumes, emotional contexts, or environments so the skill generalizes to real-life communication demands [7▪▪]. Similarly, random practice, where skills are mixed rather than practiced in a predictable sequence, reduces reliance on rote repetition and encourages flexible, adaptive control of the target voice behaviour [36]. In older adults learning ‘Twang,’ blocked practice best supported acquisition, whereas random practice tended to improve retention/transfer despite poorer immediate performance [37▪▪] In the practice phase, feedback should shift from frequent, immediate KP to less frequent, slightly delayed KR. Providing KR on only some trials (e.g., ~50%) and waiting a few seconds promotes self-evaluation and internal monitoring, supporting retention and independent skill use [7▪▪]. Giving KR on every trial in a vowel-nasalization task (100% KR) reduced accuracy and increased variability, compared with 50% KR or no KR. Meanwhile reduced/no KR improved retention (5 min) and transfer (24 h), supporting faded feedback [38]. Similarly, receiving continuous ambulatory voice biofeedback produced strongest immediate reductions in high-intensity events while summary feedback supported more stable retention of reduced vocal intensity in both healthy participants and participants with phonotraumatic vocal hyperfunction [39,40]. However, studies in speech disorders have reported equivocal findings regarding benefits of KP versus KR and high versus low frequency feedback during practice, suggesting the need to explore how these parameters interact with task, client, and context-related factors [41,42].

One key concept underlying PML-based therapies is the specificity principle, which proposes that learning is strongest when practice directly trains the exact skill to be changed and closely matches real-life performance [43]. Accordingly, therapy should emphasize the target behaviour (e.g., clear voice) rather than related behaviours (e.g., breathing patterns), use whole, authentic speech (words/conversation rather than isolated sounds), prioritize high-accuracy ‘match-like’ practice, and vary conditions (pitch, loudness, rate, context, environment, and communication partners) to promote transfer. This specificity must be balanced against task complexity. When tasks are too difficult because of demanding coordination, unfamiliar sensations, or multiple steps occurring at once, clients may feel overwhelmed and discouraged, reducing practice quality, adherence and most importantly, motivation. Therapy should therefore target a level of complexity that is at the optimal challenge level, as described in the Challenge Point Framework [44], and then follow a progression to more difficult functional tasks. A structured hierarchy supports early success while gradually increasing challenge to build competence and confidence over time [45]. This model is common, with varying numbers of levels used across different voice therapies [46–49].

Conversation training therapy offers an alternative to a hierarchical model of voice therapy [50] by leveraging the specificity principle from the outset. From the first session, patients practice conversational level connected speech, using whole-task, context-specific speech to support retention and transfer. The prepractice phase appears to occur in stimulability testing where patients demonstrate if they can produce the target, i.e. clear voice. CTT improved VHI-10 with fewer sessions and lower attrition, producing sustained patient-reported and acoustic/aerodynamic/perceptual gains in ~2 sessions [51▪▪], however, participants required stimulability (ability to hear/feel the target change) as an inclusion criterion. Conversely, research comparing cognitive depletion using pre/post Stroop test, effort ratings, and vocal outcomes (fundamental frequency, perceptual accuracy) between Resonant Voice Therapy (RVT; syllable-based) and CTT (extemporaneous speech) found that early voice therapy demands attention/self-regulation. The authors concluded that conversation-level tasks may hinder learning, and perceived effort may not match objective load [52].

One aspect of practice yet to be explored in depth is the role of negative practice [16▪,53] also known as the Old-Way, New-Way approach to technique change. Negative practice has been adapted from Lyndon's educational work targeting habitual spelling errors in students [54,55]. The purpose of the intervention is to actively contrast an old-way with learning a new-way. Different from perceptual discrimination training in the prepractice phase, this contrasting in the practice phase is proposed to reduce inhibition (also termed proactive interference) of the old on the new, thereby promoting forgetting of the old. A preliminary study has shown a nonsignificant trend that negative practice was more effective than repetitive drill for generalisation of a voice therapy task, however, the sample size was underpowered [53].

sec.title: CONSTRAINTS TO MOTOR LEARNING
sec.p: Motor learning in voice therapy can be limited by several constraints that affect a client's ability to engage with, perform, and retain new vocal behaviours. Lack of motivation is the primary constraint to learning, and task complexity a consideration needing balance with motivation and specificity, as described above. Cognitive and physical limitations can also shape how readily a client learns new motor patterns. Differences in self-regulation [56], self -efficacy, [57] attention, memory, processing speed [58], and/or sensory awareness [59] may reduce the client's ability to follow instructions, self-monitor performance, or consistently execute the target behaviour. Physical factors such as structural abnormalities of the larynx, medical conditions, fatigue [59], pain, reduced coordination or muscular conditioning or can also interfere with practice. Effective intervention therefore requires individualization. Therapists must adapt task selection, instruction, feedback type and timing, practice demands, pacing, and support strategies to match the client's strengths and needs, maximizing learning while minimizing unnecessary barriers.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: The principles of motor learning offer a comprehensive, evidence-based framework for skill acquisition and retention/generalization in voice therapy. Recent research presents evidence that there may be some variance in application of these principles in voice therapy but as yet there is no definitive evidence for novel application in specific clinical scenarios. By incorporating recommended prepractice and practice strategies from other fields of study according to the individual client needs, therapists can help clients achieve long-term retention and generalization of motor skills. While the ML may take time and require significant effort, the ultimate goal of permanent skill acquisition and transfer makes it a valuable approach for addressing complex motor challenges in voice therapy.

note.p: Evaluates the efficacy of Conversation Training Therapy (CTT) for individuals with benign vocal fold lesions and muscle tension dysphonia by comparing outcomes with matched historical control patients. The study demonstrates that therapy emphasizing natural conversational voice use can lead to meaningful improvements in voice outcomes. It provides evidence supporting functionally oriented voice therapy approaches that focus on carryover of therapeutic techniques into everyday communication.
